recommendations.reason: Fills the single flagged missing essential — a proper winter coat. The wardrobe's outerwear is entirely leather/suede/denim/varsity (formality 4-6, casual-to-statement); there is nothing tailored or genuinely warm for temperate winters. A navy single-breasted wool overcoat adds a smart, high-formality layer that instantly dresses up the pleated trousers and knitwear, introduces navy (only 1 item in palette) without breaking the neutral core, and covers the coldest end of the UK year.

The wardrobe has only one sweater (burgundy oversized mohair, a statement piece) and no plain, versatile mid-layer. A mid-weight navy wool crewneck is the workhorse knit that layers under every leather jacket, over the oxford or a tee, and stands alone with trousers or jeans — one of the largest single outfit-combination multipliers available here.

All three owned bottoms are dark (black pleated trousers, black jeans — plus the black denim jacket is outerwear), so every outfit currently anchors on a dark leg. A light beige/stone chino is the missing light-neutral bottom: it lifts the palette, provides essential contrast under the dark leather and knitwear, and pairs with virtually every top the client owns. High impact for very low spend.

The client's shirts are all casual/statement (plaid, work, striped tee) topping out around formality 4. There is no clean, smart button-up. A light-blue Italian-cotton oxford raises the formality ceiling, works under the new overcoat and the leather jackets, tucks into the pleated trousers for a polished look, and adds a soft cool tone to a black/brown-dominant palette.

The only denim owned is black, so the entire jeans rotation is one wash. A.P.C.'s raw indigo Petit New Standard is the definitive minimalist jean — it introduces a mid-blue that the wardrobe completely lacks, ages beautifully, and reads as quiet-luxury casual. It diversifies the bottom half and gives the leather jackets, knitwear and sneakers a fresh, less monochrome base to sit on.
